# Learning from Evolving Errors: Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation

Rui Li  Liyang He  Zheng Zhang  Zhenya Huang  Linbo Zhu  Qi Liu
Affiliation: University of Science and Technology of China
Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University
Email: <ruili2000@mail.ustc.edu.cn>

###### Abstract

On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) supplies dense token-level feedback
on trajectories sampled from the student’s own policy, a richer training
signal than the outcome-level rewards of reinforcement learning. This
feedback comes from a teacher conditioned on a full reference solution
unavailable to the student. The reference solution specifies the target
but not how to move from the student’s current error toward it, creating
a _solution-conditioned shortcut risk_. We introduce Air-OPD, an
adaptive iterative repair framework for on-policy distillation that
provides error-to-repair supervision. Given a failed response, a
guidance generator synthesizes repair guidance for the current error.
The student samples an on-policy retry with this guidance. If the retry
remains incorrect, the generator produces new repair guidance for the
newly observed error. At each round, a fixed teacher receives the
guidance as privileged context and supervises the student on an
error-aligned region of its latest failed response. Outcome-aware stage
weighting favors early repair stages and credits stages whose immediate
retry passes verification. We train Air-OPD on the DAPO-Math-17K dataset
and evaluate on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25, alongside
out-of-distribution tests on MMLU-Pro and GPQA. We examine two guidance
sources, self-guidance from the current student policy and external
guidance from a larger model. For both Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, Air-OPD
attains the best mathematical-reasoning averages, improving over the
strongest baseline by up to 3.6 points, while preserving base-model
performance on the out-of-distribution benchmarks.

## 1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is now a standard
approach to improving language-model reasoning in post-training ([Shao
et al., 2024](#bib.bib34); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib47)). However,
typical RLVR algorithms such as GRPO ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib7);
[Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib34)) rely on outcome rewards to compute
response-level advantages for policy optimization. Such response-level
supervision does not distinguish fine-grained token-level contributions
within a trajectory. On-policy distillation (OPD) complements this
outcome signal with dense token-level supervision on the student’s own
trajectories ([Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Lu & Thinking Machines
Lab, 2025](#bib.bib26)). On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) further
removes the need for a separate teacher model ([Zhao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib52)). Through in-context learning, the model serves as its
own teacher, conditioned on a reference solution as privileged context
that the student never observes.

Learning with privileged information uses training-only signals to guide
the learner ([Vapnik & Vashist, 2009](#bib.bib37); [Lopez-Paz et al.,
2016](#bib.bib24)). In reference-conditioned OPSD, a successful attempt
already satisfies the verifier, and further conditioning on a static
reference may steer the student toward the reference’s solution path.
Privileged supervision is thus most informative on failed attempts, and
recent work treats successful and failed trajectories asymmetrically
([Hou et al., 2026](#bib.bib11); [Zheng et al., 2026](#bib.bib53)). For
failed trajectories, a reference solution identifies the correct
destination but does not specify the transition from the student’s
current error to a valid continuation. When the teacher remains
conditioned on that same full solution, the student may learn to imitate
privileged demonstrations rather than acquire generalizable
error-correction mechanisms. We refer to this as the
_solution-conditioned shortcut risk_.

This leads to our central research question:

> _How can privileged supervision turn a failed on-policy trajectory
> into a sequence of learnable error-to-repair transitions?_

To answer this question, we introduce Air-OPD. Inspired by instructional
scaffolding ([Wood et al., 1976](#bib.bib42)), Air-OPD performs
multi-round adaptive repair that replaces a static reference-conditioned
target with repair guidance synthesized for the student’s latest error.
Given a failed response, a privileged guidance generator uses the
reference solution to synthesize repair guidance as scaffolding for the
identified error, and the student samples an on-policy retry with this
guidance. If the retry remains incorrect, the generator synthesizes
fresh repair guidance targeting the newly observed error. At every
round, the guidance serves as teacher-only privileged context for
supervising the student on its latest failed response. Air-OPD
supervises only an error-aligned repair region of that response and
excludes tokens that the repair guidance does not target, which would
otherwise add noise. Each round thus contributes one stage loss. To
combine these losses across rounds, we design outcome-aware stage
weighting, which favors earlier repair stages and rewards stages whose
retry passes verification.

We train on mathematical problems from DAPO-Math-17K ([Yu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib47)), pairing each problem with a reference solution
generated by GPT-5.5, and evaluate on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25. We
additionally test transfer beyond this mathematical training
distribution on MMLU-Pro and GPQA, and compare two guidance sources,
self-guidance from the current student policy and external guidance from
a larger model. Across these settings, Air-OPD attains the best
mathematical-reasoning averages on both Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B while
preserving base-model performance on the out-of-distribution (OOD)
benchmarks.

Our contributions are:

1.  1.  We introduce Air-OPD, an adaptive iterative repair framework that
        aligns privileged on-policy supervision with the student’s evolving
        errors. Air-OPD synthesizes error-specific repair guidance and
        updates it in response to subsequent failed on-policy attempts.
2.  2.  We develop an error-aligned distillation objective that uses newly
        synthesized guidance as privileged teacher context when scoring the
        current failed response. Each supervision region covers the span
        where the teacher still expresses correction, and outcome-aware
        stage weighting allocates supervision across repair stages.
3.  3.  Across Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B with self- and external guidance,
        Air-OPD improves average mathematical-reasoning accuracy by up to
        $`3.6`$ percentage points over the strongest evaluated baseline,
        while keeping average OOD performance near that of the base model.
        Ablations support the roles of error-aligned supervision and stage
        weighting.

## 2 Related Work

#### Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.

Building on reinforcement learning from human feedback ([Schulman
et al., 2017](#bib.bib33); [Ouyang et al., 2022](#bib.bib28)),
reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves
language-model reasoning using rewards from automatically checkable
outcomes ([Lambert et al., 2025](#bib.bib21); [Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib7); [Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib47)). DeepSeekMath
introduces Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for mathematical
reasoning ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib34)), while DAPO advances
large-scale reasoning training through improved sampling and policy
optimization ([Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib47)). Process-level rewards
densify this outcome signal by scoring intermediate steps ([Lightman
et al., 2024](#bib.bib22); [Wang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib40)), yet the
supervision remains a scalar reward rather than a token-level target.
For group-relative methods such as GRPO, difficult samples on which all
rollouts are incorrect provide no relative advantage signal for updating
the policy. To address this limitation, hint-based RL uses auxiliary
guidance to make hard problems more tractable and recover useful
training signals ([Cao et al., 2026](#bib.bib2); [Fan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib5)). StepHint guides exploration with partial solution
steps ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib49)). NuRL injects abstract hints
when independent attempts fail ([Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)), while
Scaf-GRPO provides progressively more detailed hints from a
pre-generated, fixed hint hierarchy ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib50)).
HiLL further learns hints conditioned on the reasoner’s current
failures, seeking to restore informative reward variation while
encouraging transfer to no-hint reasoning ([Xia et al.,
2026](#bib.bib43)). While these approaches use hints to reduce effective
task difficulty and recover outcome-based _reward_ signals (from fixed
pre-generated hierarchies or from a learned hinter), Air-OPD synthesizes
repair guidance for each failed response during multi-turn repair and
uses it as privileged teacher context for token-level supervision of the
repair.

#### On-policy (self-) distillation.

Knowledge distillation trains a student to match a teacher’s output
distribution ([Hinton et al., 2015](#bib.bib8); [Kim & Rush,
2016](#bib.bib15)). On-policy distillation (OPD) instead has the teacher
score responses sampled from the student’s own policy ([Ross et al.,
2011](#bib.bib32); [Lin et al., 2020](#bib.bib23); [Agarwal et al.,
2024](#bib.bib1); [Gu et al., 2024](#bib.bib6); [Ko et al.,
2024](#bib.bib17); [Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025](#bib.bib26)),
avoiding the mismatch between fixed demonstrations and the states the
student reaches at deployment. OPSD extends OPD through in-context
self-distillation, where the same model produces teacher and student
distributions under asymmetric contexts ([Zhao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib52)). In the reference-conditioned setting, the teacher
receives a reference solution that is unavailable to the student,
yielding dense token-level feedback on states that the student actually
visits. Subsequent methods adjust the strength or routing of this signal
using outcomes, reliability, or trajectory structure ([Hou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib11); [Zheng et al., 2026](#bib.bib53); [Zhang et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib51)). Closer to our setting, several distillation methods
anchor supervision at failures ([Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib44); [Wang
et al., 2026](#bib.bib39)). HINT-SD distills a feedback-conditioned
teacher on failure-relevant spans selected in hindsight ([Yeo et al.,
2026](#bib.bib46)), and TAPO inserts a diagnosis-and-correction
transition after the learner’s first critical error ([Huang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib14)). Across these methods, the corrected trajectory or
privileged context is constructed in a single pass and does not respond
to how the learner fails again. We focus on how privileged context
should be updated from one failed retry to the next.

#### Self-correction and iterative refinement.

Inference-time methods treat an initial response as an intermediate
state and use subsequent feedback to revise it. Self-Refine alternates
self-generated feedback and refinement ([Madaan et al.,
2023](#bib.bib27)), while Reflexion converts task feedback into verbal
reflections that guide later trials ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib35)).
Their effectiveness depends on the information in the feedback, as
language models struggle to identify and repair complex reasoning
mistakes without external reference signals ([Huang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib13)).

Training-time methods instead seek to internalize improvement behavior.
Self-training bootstraps from the model’s own verified rationales
([Zelikman et al., 2022](#bib.bib48); [Singh et al., 2024](#bib.bib36);
[Hosseini et al., 2024](#bib.bib10)), RISE fine-tunes on multi-turn
revision trajectories ([Qu et al., 2024](#bib.bib29)), SCoRe learns
multi-turn self-correction under the model’s own distribution via
reinforcement learning ([Kumar et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)), and
SuperCorrect distills teacher-generated thought templates and correction
traces ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib45)). Air-OPD uses iterative repair
to construct error-aligned distillation targets on the student’s own
failed responses: at each stage, a teacher conditioned on newly
synthesized repair guidance supervises the current response.

## 3 Preliminaries: On-Policy Self-Distillation

Let $`q`$ denote a problem and $`p_{\theta}`$ a trainable student policy
that defines next-token distributions given a conditioning context.
On-policy distillation (OPD) trains the student on states that it
actually visits ([Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Lu & Thinking
Machines Lab, 2025](#bib.bib26)). Given a response
$`y\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q)`$ sampled from the current policy, a
teacher $`p_{\mathrm{T}}`$ scores every token $`y_{j}`$ given its prefix
$`y_{<j}`$ (tokens indexed from $`0`$), and OPD minimizes the
token-level divergence

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}(q,y)=\frac{1}{|y|}\sum_{j=0}^{|y|-1}D\!\left(p_{\mathrm{T}}(\cdot\mid q,y_{<j})\,\big\|\,p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,y_{<j})\right).
``` |  | (1) |

Because the response is sampled from $`p_{\theta}`$, the teacher
provides dense feedback on prefixes generated by the evolving student.
In OPD, the teacher is typically a separate, more capable model.

On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) further initializes the student and
the teacher from the same model, removing the need for a separately
trained teacher ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib52)). Providing the
reference solution $`z`$ as additional input to the teacher gives it
information that the student cannot access. Here the teacher
$`p_{\mathrm{T}}`$ is instantiated as the frozen initial backbone
$`\bar{p}`$. For an on-policy response
$`y\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q)`$, distillation compares the two
branches at the same student-generated prefixes $`y_{<j}`$. The teacher
conditions on $`(q,z,y_{<j})`$, the student conditions on
$`(q,y_{<j})`$, and the OPSD loss is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPSD}}(q,z,y)=\frac{1}{|y|}\sum_{j=0}^{|y|-1}D\!\left(p_{\mathrm{T}}(\cdot\mid q,z,y_{<j})\,\big\|\,p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,y_{<j})\right),
``` |  | (2) |

where only the teacher branch observes $`z`$. Following OPSD, we
instantiate $`D`$ as the forward KL divergence
$`D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(p_{\mathrm{T}}\,\|\,p_{\theta}\right)`$ and
apply pointwise clipping, which caps each vocabulary entry’s divergence
contribution so that a few high-divergence tokens cannot dominate the
update.

In OPSD, in-context learning thus converts the reference solution into
fine-grained supervision over the probability of each token in the
student’s on-policy response. However, under this construction, the
teacher must extract relevant information from the complete reference
solution and relate it to the student’s current reasoning response. This
process is performed implicitly and does not explicitly teach the
student how to transition from its current error state to a valid
solution state.

## 4 Air-OPD: Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation

Figure 1: Overview of Air-OPD. When an on-policy rollout fails
verification, the guidance generator $`\mathcal{G}`$ quotes the first
flawed step as an error anchor $`a_{t}`$ and synthesizes repair guidance
$`g_{t}`$. A frozen teacher conditioned on $`g_{t}`$ then supervises the
student over the error-aligned repair region $`R_{t}`$, and the student
retries with the guidance in context. A verified retry ends the
trajectory, and outcome-aware stage weighting combines the stage losses
with weights $`w_{t}\propto\gamma^{t}\rho^{s_{t}}`$.

Air-OPD makes explicit the extraction step that OPSD leaves to the
teacher
(Figure [1](#S4.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 4 Air-OPD: Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")).
A guidance generator reads the reference solution and writes repair
guidance for the student’s current error, and the teacher receives this
guidance in place of the full reference solution. The rest of the method
answers three questions: how the guidance is updated across repair
rounds
(Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Multi-round adaptive repair ‣ 4 Air-OPD: Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")),
which tokens of each failed response the teacher supervises
(Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Error-aligned privileged distillation ‣ 4 Air-OPD: Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")),
and how the resulting stage losses are combined
(Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Outcome-aware stage weighting ‣ 4 Air-OPD: Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")).

### 4.1 Multi-round adaptive repair

Air-OPD performs up to $`K`$ repair rounds, adapting the guidance to the
student’s latest failed response. Let $`\mathcal{H}_{t}`$ denote the
student-visible dialogue history at stage $`t`$, with
$`\mathcal{H}_{0}`$ containing only the problem $`q`$. The student
generates an on-policy response

|     |                                                 |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       y_{t}\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{H}_{t}).
       ```                                              |     | (3) |

If $`y_{t}`$ fails verification by an outcome verifier $`V`$, the
guidance generator $`\mathcal{G}`$ uses the reference solution $`z`$ to
diagnose the current failure and produce

|     |                                                       |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       (a_{t},g_{t})=\mathcal{G}(q,z,\mathcal{H}_{t},y_{t}).
       ```                                                    |     | (4) |

Here, $`a_{t}`$ quotes the identified first flawed step verbatim, and
$`g_{t}`$ provides concise guidance for correcting it. Rule-based checks
filter out guidance that reveals the final answer
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Prompts and Validation Details ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")
details the rules).

To advance the repair process, we prompt the student to repair the
previous erroneous response $`y_{t}`$ according to $`g_{t}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{H}_{t+1}=\operatorname{Update}(\mathcal{H}_{t},y_{t},g_{t}).
``` |  | (5) |

$`\operatorname{Update}`$ appends $`y_{t}`$ to the history as the
model’s own output turn, and appends $`g_{t}`$, rendered with a repair
instruction, as the next input turn. If budget remains, the student then
generates the retry
$`y_{t+1}\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{H}_{t+1})`$; if the retry
remains incorrect, $`\mathcal{G}`$ re-localizes the error in $`y_{t+1}`$
and generates updated guidance. The process ends when a response passes
verification or the budget is exhausted. Throughout this process, the
privileged context keeps adapting to the student’s current error state.
Appendix [D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Worked repair examples ‣ Appendix D Additional Results and Examples ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")
presents worked repair examples from training.

### 4.2 Error-aligned privileged distillation

At stage $`t`$, the teacher and student score the same failed response
$`y_{t}`$ under the shared dialogue history $`\mathcal{H}_{t}`$. The
frozen teacher $`p_{\mathrm{T}}`$ additionally receives the newly
generated guidance $`g_{t}`$, which is withheld from the student when
scoring $`y_{t}`$.

To cover both the current error and the potentially recoverable region
that follows, the supervision region starts at the beginning of the
error region. We exactly match $`a_{t}`$ against $`y_{t}`$ to obtain the
start position $`b_{t}`$. Supervising the error region alone would lose
this recoverable region, so we rely on the corrective signal from the
teacher to determine the endpoint of the supervision region. At position
$`j`$, we measure this signal as the total positive teacher–student
probability difference over alternatives to the observed token:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
C_{t,j}=\sum_{v\neq y_{t,j}}\left[p_{\mathrm{T}}\!\left(v\mid\mathcal{H}_{t},g_{t},y_{t,<j}\right)-p_{\theta}\!\left(v\mid\mathcal{H}_{t},y_{t,<j}\right)\right]_{+}.
``` |  | (6) |

Both distributions are already computed for the stage loss, so measuring
this signal introduces no additional computational overhead.

To avoid ending the region within a reasoning block, we partition the
suffix of $`y_{t}`$ starting at $`b_{t}`$ at blank-line boundaries. Let
$`\mathcal{E}_{t}`$ denote the resulting block endpoints, including the
response end $`|y_{t}|`$. For a tolerance $`\epsilon\in(0,1)`$, we
select the earliest endpoint retaining at least a $`1-\epsilon`$
fraction of the suffix’s total corrective signal:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
e_{t}=\min\Bigl\{r\in\mathcal{E}_{t}:\textstyle\sum_{j=b_{t}}^{r-1}C_{t,j}\geq(1-\epsilon)\textstyle\sum_{j=b_{t}}^{|y_{t}|-1}C_{t,j}\Bigr\}.
``` |  | (7) |

By construction, the discarded tail carries at most an $`\epsilon`$
fraction of the suffix’s total corrective signal. If the total signal is
zero, we retain the full suffix. Following
Eq. [2](#S3.E2 "In 3 Preliminaries: On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation"),
the stage loss averages the divergence over the selected repair region
$`R_{t}=y_{t}[b_{t}:e_{t}]`$, i.e., tokens $`b_{t}`$ to $`e_{t}-1`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{t}=\frac{1}{e_{t}-b_{t}}\sum_{j=b_{t}}^{e_{t}-1}D\!\left(p_{\mathrm{T}}\!\left(\cdot\mid\mathcal{H}_{t},g_{t},y_{t,<j}\right)\,\big\|\,p_{\theta}\!\left(\cdot\mid\mathcal{H}_{t},y_{t,<j}\right)\right).
``` |  | (8) |

Gradients flow only through the student branch.

### 4.3 Outcome-aware stage weighting

Training samples contain different numbers of repair stages, and
directly summing stage losses would grant samples with more repair
rounds a larger total weight. To avoid this, we introduce *outcome-aware
stage weighting*. The scheme allocates the stage weights within each
supervised trajectory by stage depth and the outcome of the retry
immediately following each stage.

This allocation rests on two assumptions about the repair process.
First, imperfect retries accumulate noise across stages. The later a
stage is, the more failed responses and repair guidance accumulate in
its context and the less reliable its supervision signal becomes, so the
weights should lean toward earlier stages. Second, whether the immediate
retry passes verification reflects the stage’s supervision quality. A
successful retry indicates that the stage’s repair guidance pointed to a
valid repair, and such a stage should receive an additional weight
bonus.

Concretely, for trajectory $`n`$ with final supervised stage $`T_{n}`$
and stage losses $`\mathcal{L}_{n,t}`$
(Eq. [8](#S4.E8 "In 4.2 Error-aligned privileged distillation ‣ 4 Air-OPD: Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")),
let $`s_{n,t}=\mathds{1}[V(y_{n,t+1})=1]`$ indicate whether the
on-policy retry immediately following stage $`t`$ passes the outcome
verifier $`V`$, with $`s_{n,t}=0`$ when no retry is available (after the
final round). The stage weights are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{gathered}w_{n,t}=\frac{\widetilde{w}_{n,t}}{\sum_{k=0}^{T_{n}}\widetilde{w}_{n,k}},\qquad\widetilde{w}_{n,t}=\gamma^{t}\rho^{s_{n,t}},\\
\gamma\in(0,1],\qquad\rho\geq 1.\end{gathered}
``` |  | (9) |

The temporal factor $`\gamma^{t}`$ (with $`\gamma<1`$) decays the
weights with stage depth, the outcome bonus $`\rho^{s_{n,t}}`$ rewards a
verified immediate retry, and the normalization gives each supervised
trajectory unit total weight.

For a minibatch of repair trajectories $`\mathcal{B}`$, the final
objective is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\textsc{Air-OPD}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{n\in\mathcal{B}}\sum_{t=0}^{T_{n}}w_{n,t}\mathcal{L}_{n,t}.
``` |  | (10) |

The complete algorithm is summarized in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Complete Training Algorithm ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation").

## 5 Experimental Setup

### 5.1 Models, training data, and baselines

We use two Qwen variants of different scales, Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B
([Qwen Team, 2025](#bib.bib30)). We train on the DAPO-Math-17K dataset
([Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib47)), generating the reference solution for
each problem with GPT-5.5 and retaining the 15,650 problems whose
generated solution verifies against the dataset answer. Outcome
verification at every repair round uses rule-based answer matching. We
compare *self-guidance* generated by the current student policy with
*external guidance* generated by a larger model (Qwen3.5-27B). The main
baselines are the corresponding base model and three trained methods.
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) trains on the reference solutions with a
cross-entropy loss. GRPO optimizes rule-based outcome rewards over
groups of on-policy rollouts. OPSD distills a reference-conditioned
teacher on the student’s own rollouts. All trained baselines are our
reproductions on the same training corpus and backbones
(Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Training and Evaluation Details ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")).

### 5.2 Evaluation benchmarks and metrics

We evaluate models along two dimensions, mathematical reasoning and
out-of-distribution generalization. Mathematical reasoning is evaluated
on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25 ([HMMT, 2025](#bib.bib9)). Each
mathematical benchmark contains 30 problems. We report per-benchmark
accuracy as Avg@12, with *Math Avg.* the unweighted mean of the three
benchmark scores. Out-of-distribution evaluation uses MMLU-Pro ([Wang
et al., 2024b](#bib.bib41)) and GPQA ([Rein et al., 2024](#bib.bib31))
to assess transfer beyond the mathematical training distribution,
reporting accuracy as Avg@4, with *OOD Avg.* the mean of the two
benchmarks. During evaluation, no repair guidance is added to the model
input.

### 5.3 Implementation details

We adopt the OPSD training recipe ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib52)),
using the frozen initial backbone with its adapters disabled as the
distillation teacher. During training, the student operates in
non-thinking mode and the teacher in thinking mode. Optimization uses
rank-64 LoRA adapters ([Hu et al., 2022](#bib.bib12)) and AdamW
([Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019](#bib.bib25)) with a learning rate of
$`5\times 10^{-6}`$ and an effective batch size of 32.

Air-OPD is built on TRL ([von Werra et al., 2020](#bib.bib38)) and
trains for 100 optimizer steps. Each problem allows at most $`K=3`$
adaptive repair rounds, and each round samples a single on-policy
rollout from the current student (temperature 1.1, top-$`p`$ 0.95),
capped at 8,192 tokens. Sampler weights are synchronized after every
optimizer step. The default stage weighting is
$`(\gamma,\rho)=(0.8,1.5)`$, and the endpoint budget is
$`\epsilon=0.1`$. Both guidance sources are generated in thinking mode
(temperature 0.7, top-$`p`$ 0.9) and filtered by the same validation
rules. All experiments are conducted on a single node with eight H100
GPUs.
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Training and Evaluation Details ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")
documents the complete training and evaluation configuration.

## 6 Main Results

Air-OPD achieves the best mathematical reasoning at both scales.
Table [1](#S6.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 6 Main Results ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")
compares Air-OPD against the base model, SFT, GRPO, and OPSD. Both
guidance settings surpass every baseline on Math Avg., and external
guidance, where a stronger generator supplies higher-quality repair
guidance, exceeds the strongest baseline, OPSD, by 3.6 and 2.7 points at
4B and 8B, respectively. The improvement is consistent across
benchmarks. Air-OPD variants attain the best score on every mathematical
benchmark at both scales, with pronounced gains on HMMT25.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | Mathematical Reasoning |  |  |  | Out-of-Distribution |  |  |
| Method | AIME24 | AIME25 | HMMT25 | Math Avg. | MMLU-Pro | GPQA | OOD Avg. |
| Qwen3-4B |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| Base model | 75.0 | 66.4 | 42.2 | 61.2 | 51.5 | 62.9 | 57.2 |
| SFT | 70.6 | 61.4 | 42.8 | 58.2 | 43.1 | 52.0 | 47.6 |
| GRPO | 75.6 | 67.5 | 43.9 | 62.3 | 51.3 | 62.4 | 56.8 |
| OPSD | 76.4 | 69.4 | 43.3 | 63.1 | 50.4 | 60.2 | 55.3 |
| Air-OPD (Self-G) | 76.7 | 73.1 | 47.8 | 65.8 | 52.5 | 61.4 | 56.9 |
| Air-OPD (External-G) | 80.0 | 73.3 | 46.7 | 66.7 | 51.7 | 61.9 | 56.8 |
| Qwen3-8B |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| Base model | 75.8 | 65.6 | 43.9 | 61.8 | 57.9 | 64.1 | 61.0 |
| SFT | 75.3 | 63.6 | 43.6 | 60.8 | 46.5 | 55.8 | 51.2 |
| GRPO | 76.9 | 69.2 | 45.8 | 64.0 | 56.6 | 64.5 | 60.6 |
| OPSD | 77.8 | 69.7 | 46.7 | 64.7 | 57.4 | 61.7 | 59.6 |
| Air-OPD (Self-G) | 78.3 | 72.5 | 49.7 | 66.9 | 58.3 | 63.5 | 60.9 |
| Air-OPD (External-G) | 79.7 | 73.1 | 49.4 | 67.4 | 58.0 | 64.1 | 61.1 |

Table 1: Main results on mathematical-reasoning (Avg@12) and
out-of-distribution (Avg@4) benchmarks. Both Air-OPD variants surpass
all baselines on Math Avg. at each scale while preserving base-model
performance on the OOD group. Self-G/External-G generate repair guidance
with the current student policy and Qwen3.5-27B, respectively.
Bold/underlined: best/second-best within each block.

Self-guidance alone accounts for most of the improvement. Without
introducing any external model, the self-guided variant already improves
over OPSD by 2.8 and 2.1 Math Avg. points. External guidance further
improves the Math Avg. The additional gain from external guidance is
smaller at 8B than at 4B, possibly because the larger student generates
better repair guidance itself.

Air-OPD attains stronger mathematical reasoning while preserving
near-base OOD performance. SFT lowers the OOD average by 9.6 and 9.8
points at 4B and 8B, consistent with forgetting under task-specific
fine-tuning ([Kirkpatrick et al., 2017](#bib.bib16); [Kotha et al.,
2024](#bib.bib18)), and OPSD also regresses at both scales. In contrast,
Air-OPD stays within 0.4 points of the base model at 4B and within 0.1
points at 8B. It is the only evaluated reference-based training method
that maintains a near-base OOD average at both scales. GRPO preserves
OOD performance comparably, but its Math Avg. trails Air-OPD by
$`2.9`$–$`4.4`$ points. One possible explanation lies in the granularity
of supervision. RLVR provides only scalar feedback, and full-response
distillation supervises every token, whereas Air-OPD provides corrective
signals only on regions aligned with the student’s errors. This
selective supervision may limit over-specialization to the mathematical
training distribution while preserving the gains of distillation.

## 7 Ablations and Analysis

All ablations start from the default Qwen3-4B configuration of
Section [5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Implementation details ‣ 5 Experimental Setup ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")
and report the in-domain Math Avg. We organize the analysis into three
parts.
Section [7.1](#S7.SS1 "7.1 Effect of sample selection, supervision region, and stage weighting ‣ 7 Ablations and Analysis ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")
controls for failure-only sample selection and ablates the supervision
region and the stage weighting of the objective,
Section [7.2](#S7.SS2 "7.2 Effect of the repair budget ‣ 7 Ablations and Analysis ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")
measures how large a repair budget is needed, and
Section [7.3](#S7.SS3 "7.3 Training dynamics ‣ 7 Ablations and Analysis ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")
traces how capability evolves over the course of training relative to
GRPO and OPSD.

### 7.1 Effect of sample selection, supervision region, and stage weighting

In
Table [2](#S7.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 7.1 Effect of sample selection, supervision region, and stage weighting ‣ 7 Ablations and Analysis ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation"),
the two OPSD rows vary which rollouts are supervised, and each remaining
row changes one component of Air-OPD, the supervision region
(Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Error-aligned privileged distillation ‣ 4 Air-OPD: Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation"))
or the stage weighting
(Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Outcome-aware stage weighting ‣ 4 Air-OPD: Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")),
while keeping the rest of the default configuration.

|                                    |           |
|------------------------------------|-----------|
| Setting                            | Math Avg. |
| Air-OPD                            | 65.8      |
| Sample selection (OPSD)            |           |
| All rollouts                       | 63.1      |
| Failed rollouts only               | 62.5      |
| Supervision region                 |           |
| w/o error alignment                | 64.7      |
| Error block only                   | 64.2      |
| Stage weighting $`(\gamma,\rho)`$  |           |
| Uniform $`(1,\,1)`$                | 65.0      |
| Temporal factor only $`(0.8,\,1)`$ | 65.4      |
| Outcome bonus only $`(1,\,1.5)`$   | 65.4      |

Table 2: Ablation results (Qwen3-4B, Self-G). We test failure-only
sample selection for OPSD and ablate the supervision region and the
stage-weighting components of Air-OPD.

Sample selection. Air-OPD supervises only failed rollouts, so its gains
could stem from this selection alone. Applying the OPSD loss only to
failed rollouts yields 62.5, 0.6 points below standard OPSD and 3.3
below Air-OPD. The gains thus depend on how Air-OPD supervises each
failure, not on which rollouts it selects.

Supervision region. We compare the default repair region $`R_{t}`$ with
two ablations. *W/o error alignment* supervises every token of the
failed response in place of this region, and *error block only* ends the
region at the boundary of the first reasoning block. Both ablations
lower the Math Avg. Widening supervision to the full response costs 1.1
points, and narrowing it to the error block alone costs 1.6. We suspect
that full-response supervision dilutes the signal with tokens the repair
guidance does not target, while the error block alone omits downstream
reasoning that may also require correction. These results support
supervising both the identified error region and the selected downstream
reasoning.

Figure 2: Effect of the repair budget $`K`$ (Qwen3-4B). Math Avg. (left
axis) rises through the default $`K=3`$ and then flattens, while each
variant’s number of supervised stages (dashed, right axis; % of the
samples OPSD supervises) grows with diminishing increments.

Stage weighting. We ablate the temporal factor $`\gamma^{t}`$ and the
outcome bonus $`\rho^{s_{n,t}}`$ of
Eq. [9](#S4.E9 "In 4.3 Outcome-aware stage weighting ‣ 4 Air-OPD: Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation").
*Uniform* $`(1,1)`$ removes both factors and weights all stages equally,
while *temporal factor only* $`(0.8,1)`$ and *outcome bonus only*
$`(1,1.5)`$ each restore a single factor. Either factor alone already
improves over uniform weighting, and combining the two performs best.
This indicates that the weights should combine a preference for earlier
stages with feedback from the immediate retry outcome rather than
allocate supervision by a single criterion.

### 7.2 Effect of the repair budget

We vary the maximum number of repair rounds $`K\in\{1,\ldots,5\}`$ for
both guidance settings.
Figure [2](#S7.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 7.1 Effect of sample selection, supervision region, and stage weighting ‣ 7 Ablations and Analysis ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")
traces Math Avg. as the budget grows alongside the number of supervised
stages. Both variants already surpass OPSD with a single repair round,
and the overall trend rises and then flattens. At $`K=1`$ every
supervised trajectory contains exactly one stage, so this gain does not
depend on additional repair rounds. $`K=1`$ also exceeds failure-only
OPSD by 1.1–1.5 points
(Table [2](#S7.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 7.1 Effect of sample selection, supervision region, and stage weighting ‣ 7 Ablations and Analysis ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")),
suggesting that error-aligned repair supervision provides a stronger
learning signal than reference-conditioned full-response distillation.
Raising the budget to $`K=3`$ brings further gains, which confirms the
value of continuing to supply fresh repair signals for unresolved
failures during training. Beyond this point both curves show diminishing
returns. $`K=4`$ adds only a small improvement, and $`K=5`$ falls
slightly below $`K=4`$. We suspect that stages added at deep rounds
carry accumulated noise, as their contexts pile up failed attempts and
guidance, and their less reliable supervision begins to offset the
gains.

The dashed curves show that the number of supervised stages keeps
increasing with $`K`$ but with shrinking increments, as later rounds
activate only for trajectories that remain incorrect and yield validated
repair guidance rather than for all trajectories. The count rises from
22.2% of the samples OPSD supervises at $`K=1`$ to 35.2–37.4% at
$`K=5`$. We keep $`K=3`$ as the practical default. It captures most of
the observed gains while requiring fewer supervised stages than larger
budgets. Comparing the two dashed curves further shows that external
guidance adds fewer supervised stages per extra round than
self-guidance, possibly because higher-quality external guidance
resolves more failures in earlier rounds.

Figure 3: Training dynamics on the mathematical benchmarks (Qwen3-4B).
Both Air-OPD variants lead OPSD and GRPO on the three-benchmark average
from the first checkpoint onward. Curves show Avg@12 at checkpoints
saved every 20 optimizer steps, and dashed lines mark the base model.

### 7.3 Training dynamics

Figure [3](#S7.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 7.2 Effect of the repair budget ‣ 7 Ablations and Analysis ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")
plots the three-benchmark average and per-benchmark accuracy over the
checkpoints of both Air-OPD variants, OPSD, and GRPO, saved every 20
optimizer steps, with the base model as a fixed reference. On the
three-benchmark average, both Air-OPD variants lead both baselines at
every checkpoint, and external guidance matches or exceeds the
self-guided average throughout. Air-OPD also converges substantially
faster. By step 40, both variants already reach the score OPSD attains
at step 100. This faster convergence also uses much less supervision. At
the default $`K=3`$, the number of stages supervised by Air-OPD is
approximately one third of the number of samples supervised by OPSD
(Section [7.2](#S7.SS2 "7.2 Effect of the repair budget ‣ 7 Ablations and Analysis ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")),
with each stage covering an error-aligned repair region rather than a
full response. This suggests that supervision concentrated on erroneous
regions yields more learning signal per supervised token.

## 8 Conclusion

We introduced Air-OPD, an adaptive iterative repair framework for
on-policy distillation that addresses the solution-conditioned shortcut
risk of reference-privileged supervision. Instead of conditioning the
teacher on a static reference solution, a guidance generator synthesizes
answer-free repair guidance that evolves with the student’s errors, the
teacher distills each repair over an error-aligned region of the latest
failed response, and outcome-aware stage weighting allocates supervision
across rounds. Across two model scales, both guidance sources surpass
strong RL and distillation baselines on mathematical reasoning while
preserving base-model performance out of distribution, and self-guidance
alone accounts for most of the improvement. Our analysis further shows
that the gains emerge from the first checkpoints of training, and that a
small repair budget captures most of the gains observed in our sweep
while supervising roughly a third as many samples as OPSD.

## Appendix A Complete Training Algorithm

Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix A Complete Training Algorithm ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")
gives the complete procedure that Air-OPD runs on one training
minibatch, from the initial on-policy rollouts to the returned training
loss. The method definitions and design rationale remain in
Section [4](#S4 "4 Air-OPD: Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation").

1:  Input: minibatch $`\mathcal{B}`$ of problems $`q`$ with reference
solutions $`z`$, student $`p_{\theta}`$, frozen teacher
$`p_{\mathrm{T}}`$, outcome verifier $`V`$, and guidance generator
$`\mathcal{G}`$

2:  Hyperparameters: repair budget $`K`$, endpoint tolerance
$`\epsilon\in(0,1)`$, temporal factor $`\gamma\in(0,1]`$, and outcome
bonus $`\rho\geq 1`$

3:  Output: minibatch training loss $`\mathcal{L}_{\textsc{Air-OPD}}`$

4:  for all $`(q,z)\in\mathcal{B}`$, indexed by $`n`$ do

5:   $`\mathcal{S}_{n}\leftarrow\varnothing`$,
$`\mathcal{L}_{n}\leftarrow 0`$, $`t\leftarrow 0`$,
$`\mathcal{H}_{0}\leftarrow\operatorname{Render}(q)`$, and sample
$`y_{0}\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{H}_{0})`$

6:   while $`t<K`$ and $`y_{t}`$ is a well-formed response with
$`V(y_{t})=0`$ do

7:    $`(a_{t},g_{t})\leftarrow\mathcal{G}(q,z,\mathcal{H}_{t},y_{t})`$

8:    if $`(a_{t},g_{t})`$ fails validation then

9:     break

10:    end if

11:    $`b_{t}\leftarrow`$ the exact match position of $`a_{t}`$ in
$`y_{t}`$

12:    $`e_{t}\leftarrow`$ the earliest block endpoint with corrective
coverage $`1-\epsilon`$

13:    Compute $`\mathcal{L}_{n,t}`$ on the repair region
$`R_{t}=y_{t}[b_{t}:e_{t}]`$ and add $`(t,\mathcal{L}_{n,t})`$ to
$`\mathcal{S}_{n}`$

14:
   $`\mathcal{H}_{t+1}\leftarrow\operatorname{Update}(\mathcal{H}_{t},y_{t},g_{t})`$
and, if $`t<K-1`$, sample
$`y_{t+1}\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{H}_{t+1})`$

15:    $`s_{n,t}\leftarrow\mathds{1}[V(y_{t+1})=1]`$, or $`0`$ if no
retry is sampled, and $`t\leftarrow t+1`$

16:   end while

17:   if $`\mathcal{S}_{n}\neq\varnothing`$ then

18:    $`T_{n}\leftarrow t-1`$

19:
   $`w_{n,t}\leftarrow\gamma^{t}\rho^{s_{n,t}}\big/\sum_{k=0}^{T_{n}}\gamma^{k}\rho^{s_{n,k}}`$
for $`t=0,\ldots,T_{n}`$

20:
   $`\mathcal{L}_{n}\leftarrow\sum_{t=0}^{T_{n}}w_{n,t}\mathcal{L}_{n,t}`$

21:   end if

22:  end for

23:  return
$`\mathcal{L}_{\textsc{Air-OPD}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{n\in\mathcal{B}}\mathcal{L}_{n}`$

Algorithm 1 Air-OPD: multi-round repair and stage-weighted distillation

## Appendix B Prompts and Validation Details

### B.1 Guidance generator instruction

Figures [4](#A2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ B.1 Guidance generator instruction ‣ Appendix B Prompts and Validation Details ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")
and [5](#A2.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ B.1 Guidance generator instruction ‣ Appendix B Prompts and Validation Details ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")
show the full user templates of the guidance generator for the first
repair round and for the later rounds. At every round the generator
receives the problem, the reference solution and its final answer as
privileged checking evidence, and the latest failed response. From the
second round it also receives the guidance the student has already seen.
Braced fields are filled at runtime.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 4: Guidance generator, first repair round. The template diagnoses
the initial failed response $`y_{0}`$ under the privileged reference
solution and final answer.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 5: Guidance generator, later repair rounds. The template replaces
the current guidance after a retry that is still incorrect, and
additionally receives the guidance the student has already seen.

### B.2 Repair dialogue

The retry is sampled from a multi-turn dialogue whose turns are shown
below. The initial user turn poses the problem, and each unsuccessful
response is followed by a feedback turn that delivers the current repair
guidance. From the second feedback turn onward the opening line instead
reads The previous answer is still incorrect.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### B.3 Validation rules

The generator output is accepted only when it matches one of the two
declared forms in full, with a nonempty error quote and a nonempty
repair-guidance field. The error quote must be located in the latest
response, and guidance that states the final answer is rejected. The
leak check excludes the error quote and rejects guidance containing
boxed answers or rule-based matches to the normalized reference answer,
such as explicit answer statements or variable assignments. These
surface-form checks do not guarantee detection of all semantic answer
leakage. When any check fails, or when the generator returns no_repair,
the round yields no supervised stage and stops further retries.

## Appendix C Training and Evaluation Details

### C.1 Training settings

Following the comparison setup of OPSD ([Zhao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib52)),
Table [3](#A3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ C.1 Training settings ‣ Appendix C Training and Evaluation Details ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")
places SFT, GRPO, OPSD, and Air-OPD side by side, grouping their
optimization and on-policy sampling settings. All trained baselines in
Table [1](#S6.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 6 Main Results ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")
are our own reproductions on the same training corpus and backbones as
Air-OPD; the GRPO reproduction applies no KL penalty, and the untrained
base-model row has no optimization settings. Training problems come from
DAPO-Math-17K ([Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib47)), and outcome verification
at every repair round uses rule-based answer matching. Reference
solutions are generated by GPT-5.5 and retained only when their final
answers verify against the dataset answers, leaving 15,650 of the 17,398
problems as training rows. SFT minimizes cross-entropy on these
reference solutions without on-policy sampling and uses a 16,000-token
maximum sequence length measured over the full supervised sequence.

All trained methods are implemented on top of TRL ([von Werra et al.,
2020](#bib.bib38)) and use AdamW, BF16, and FlashAttention-2 ([Dao,
2024](#bib.bib4)), with a colocated vLLM sampler ([Kwon et al.,
2023](#bib.bib20)) for on-policy rollouts. For OPSD and Air-OPD, the
pointwise divergence-clipping threshold is $`\tau=0.05`$.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  Parameter | SFT | GRPO | OPSD | Air-OPD |
| Optimization and adaptation |  |  |  |  |
|  Optimizer | AdamW | AdamW | AdamW | AdamW |
|  Learning rate | $`5\times 10^{-6}`$ | $`5\times 10^{-6}`$ | $`5\times 10^{-6}`$ | $`5\times 10^{-6}`$ |
|  Effective batch size | 32 | 32 | 32 | 32 |
|  Training precision | BF16 | BF16 | BF16 | BF16 |
|  LoRA rank / alpha | 64 / 128 | 64 / 128 | 64 / 128 | 64 / 128 |
|  Optimizer steps | 100 | 500 | 100 | 100 |
|  SFT maximum sequence length | 16,000 | – | – | – |
| On-policy sampling |  |  |  |  |
|  Maximum completion length | – | 16,000 | 8,192 | 8,192 |
|  Rollouts per prompt / dialogue state | – | 8 | 1 | 1 |
|  Sampling temperature | – | 1.2 | 1.1 | 1.1 |

Table 3: Training settings for SFT, GRPO, OPSD, and Air-OPD. Lengths are
measured in tokens; the SFT limit applies to the full supervised
sequence. A dash denotes a setting that is not applicable. For Air-OPD,
one rollout is sampled per dialogue state: the initial response can be
followed by at most $`K-1`$ retries.

#### Air-OPD-specific settings.

Air-OPD adds a repair loop and a guidance generator on top of the shared
configuration in
Table [3](#A3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ C.1 Training settings ‣ Appendix C Training and Evaluation Details ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation").
Each problem allows at most $`K=3`$ repair rounds, with stage weighting
$`(\gamma,\rho)=(0.8,1.5)`$ and endpoint tolerance $`\epsilon=0.1`$. The
student decodes with top-$`p`$ 0.95 and top-$`k`$ 20, generating at most
8,192 completion tokens under a total sequence-length limit of 19,168
tokens. Self-guidance from the current student policy and external
guidance from Qwen3.5-27B share the same inference settings. Both
generate with thinking mode enabled, a temperature of 0.7, top-$`p`$
0.9, and at most 8,192 new tokens.

### C.2 Inference settings

Table [4](#A3.T4 "Table 4 ‣ C.2 Inference settings ‣ Appendix C Training and Evaluation Details ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")
summarizes the inference settings shared by the base model and all
trained methods for mathematical-reasoning evaluation. We use the fixed
random seed 2026 to generate 12 responses per problem, with a sampling
temperature of 1.0, top-$`p`$ 0.95, no top-$`k`$ restriction, a maximum
of 38,912 new tokens, a model context length of 40,960, and thinking
enabled. Following the OPSD evaluation protocol ([Zhao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib52)), we evaluate checkpoints every 20 steps up to 100
steps. Overall Math Avg. is the macro-average of the three mathematical
benchmark scores.

|                                 |         |
|---------------------------------|---------|
|  Parameter                      | Value   |
|  Maximum new tokens             | 38,912  |
|  Maximum model length (tokens)  | 40,960  |
|  Thinking mode                  | Enabled |
|  Sampling temperature           | 1.0     |
|  Top-$`p`$                      | 0.95    |
|  Top-$`k`$                      | –       |
|  Samples per problem            | 12      |
|  Random seed                    | 2026    |

Table 4: Inference settings for mathematical-reasoning evaluation. The
base model and all trained methods use these settings on AIME24, AIME25,
and HMMT25, without repair guidance.

#### Out-of-distribution evaluation.

MMLU-Pro is evaluated on a fixed 1,000-question subset that covers all
14 subject categories, and GPQA on the 198-question GPQA-Diamond split.
For the base model and every trained method, both benchmarks draw four
samples per question (Avg@4) with a sampling temperature of 1.0,
top-$`p`$ 0.95, no top-$`k`$ restriction, and the random seed
2026071201. MMLU-Pro applies the chat template with thinking enabled, a
maximum of 8,192 new tokens, and a model context length of 12,288. GPQA
feeds the question prompt to the model without the chat template, with a
maximum of 38,912 new tokens and a model context length of 40,960. The
predicted option is read from the last \boxed{} in the response, and
MMLU-Pro additionally accepts an explicit final-answer statement.

## Appendix D Additional Results and Examples

### D.1 Worked repair examples

We reconstruct two complete repair trajectories from the training-time
repair logs of the Qwen3-4B self-guidance run, both repaired at the
second round. In the first the retry fixes the anchored slip but returns
the identical wrong answer, and in the second the retry adopts the
corrected equation yet slips again in the very next step although the
guidance is valid. The two trajectories illustrate the rationale of the
outcome-aware stage weighting in
Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Outcome-aware stage weighting ‣ 4 Air-OPD: Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation").
Because a retry can fail even under valid guidance, a failed retry is
not penalized, and the weighting grants its outcome bonus only to the
stage whose guidance leads to the verified repair. In each round box,
the error anchor $`a_{t}`$ located by the guidance generator is
highlighted in the failed response, and the supervised repair region
$`R_{t}`$ opens at the anchor and ends at the endpoint
Eq. [7](#S4.E7 "In 4.2 Error-aligned privileged distillation ‣ 4 Air-OPD: Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation ‣ Learning from Evolving Errors:Adaptive Iterative Repair for On-Policy Distillation")
selects for that stage. Elisions are marked $`[\ldots]`$.

#### Example 1: repaired in two rounds.

The initial attempt counts $`\binom{20}{2}=190`$ choices for Terry and
$`\binom{18}{2}=153`$ for Mary but writes the product as $`29{,}170`$,
counts only the two-red and two-blue cases, and reduces the resulting
fraction with a faulty remainder chain to $`12/139`$, answering $`151`$.
The first-round guidance anchors the earliest error, the multiplication
slip; the retry corrects the product to $`29{,}070`$ yet repeats the
earlier remainder chain during the reduction and returns the identical
$`151`$, so $`s_{0}=0`$. The second-round guidance targets the remaining
omission, the mixed one-red-one-blue case, and the following retry sums
all three cases and reaches the verified $`441`$, so $`s_{1}=1`$.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Example 2: a retry that fails under valid guidance.

The initial attempt equates the binomial probabilities of exactly two
and exactly three heads but mishandles the $`(3/4)`$ exponent while
cancelling the common factor, reducing the equality to
$`\binom{n}{2}=\binom{n}{3}\cdot\frac{3}{16}`$ and reaching $`n=18`$.
The first-round guidance anchors this equation and derives the correct
coefficient $`\frac{1}{3}`$. The retry derives the correct equation but
mishandles the right-hand side while clearing denominators. The next
guidance recommends multiplying by 18 to clear all denominators in one
step, after which the retry succeeds.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
````
